identity.author: John Davenant
identity.work: Two Dissertations (De praedestinatione through Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol)

scope.locus: De praedestinatione Cap. IX Arg. 13 ministers sluggish / Corvinus.
scope.next_locus: Cap. IX Arg. 14 (Corvinus next argument after ministers-sluggish).

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 (Corvinus): reprobation from mere liberty of will makes ministers sluggish — diligence profits only the absolutely elect; negligence harms only those absolutely to perish
english: Our doctrine, says Corvinus, of reprobating some from mere liberty of divine will — not from foresight of final demerits in the reprobate themselves — makes God's ministers sluggish in their work. From it, he says, it follows that their diligence can profit only those God absolutely wills to save, who cannot perish; and that their negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, who cannot be saved. Admit that dogma, and ministers of the word must turn idle and torpid.
sections.latin: Nostra doctrina, inquit Corvinus, de reprobatione quorundam ex mera libertate Divinae voluntatis, et non ex praevisione finalium demeritorum in ipsis reprobatis, Dei ministros in suo ministerio segnes reddit; utpote ex qua sequatur, ipsorum diligentiam non posse prodesse nisi iis quos Deus absolute vult servare, et qui perire non possunt; et negligentiam rursus ipsorum non posse nocere nisi iis, quos Deus absolute vult perdere, quique non possunt servari: Necesse autem est, hoc dogmate admisso, inertes et torpidos reddi verbi ministros.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: even if some ministers grew sluggish, the doctrine is not thereby false — abuse of Paul's teaching and of divine foresight (Augustine's monk) does not silence truth
english: I answer: even if some ministers grew sluggish from it, that does not make the doctrine itself false or evil. From Paul's teaching some took occasion for license, saying, Let us do evil that good may come. From the doctrine of divine foresight, Augustine tells of a monk who, when the brethren corrected him for doing what he should not and leaving undone what he should, answered again and again: Whatever I am now, I shall one day be what God foresaw I would be. That monk spoke truth — and used that truth not for good but for evil. For such little objections, then, what is truly said of predestination and reprobation is neither to be denied nor kept silent.
sections.latin: Respondeo, etsi inde ministri nonnulli segnes redderentur, non tamen efficitur doctrinam in se falsam aut malam esse. Ex Pauli doctrina nonnulli captabant occasionem licentiae, dicentes, Faciamus mala ut veniant bona. Ex doctrina praescientiae Divinae, fuit quidam Monachus (referente Augustino) qui corripientibus fratribus cum quaedam non facienda faceret, et facienda non faceret, identidem respondebat, Qualiscunque nunc sim, talis olim ero qualem me Deus futurum esse praescivit. Ille Monachus et verum dicebat, et hoc vero non proficiebat in bonum, sed in malum. Propter hujusmodi igitur objectiunculas ea quae de praedestinatione ac reprobatione vera dicuntur, nec neganda sunt, nec tacenda.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: Arminius's reprobation makes ministers as sluggish — eternal foresight still fixes an immovable decree before the foundation of the world
english: Further: Arminius's view of reprobation makes ministers as sluggish as ours. However he sets predestination from foreseen faith and reprobation from foresight of unbelief, he still confesses that divine foresight eternal — and with it intervening, he acknowledges an eternal, fixed, immovable decree of election or reprobation for each person, set before the world's foundations were laid. So a minister cannot hope by diligence to lead to everlasting life someone thus reprobated from eternity, unless he also believes he can make divine foresight err and revoke God's eternal decree. Whether reprobation is set from mere liberty of divine will before all extrinsic causes, or from foresight of unbelief after consideration, it is the same: no hearer but is from eternity predestined to this side or that, from which he will never be transferred to the other.
sections.latin: Porro sententia Arminii de reprobatione tam segnes reddit ministros quam nostra. Nam utcunque ille ponat praedestinationem ex praevisa fide, et reprobationem ex praevisione infidelitatis, tamen hanc praevisionem Divinam aeternam fatetur, eademque interveniente, aeternum, fixum, et immobile decretum, sive electionis sive reprobationis, quoad singulos homines ante jacta mundi fundamenta constitutum agnoscit. Minister igitur sperare non potest se aliquem ab aeterno sic reprobatum posse sua diligentia ad vitam aeternam perducere, nisi simul credat posse se efficere ut Divina praescientia fallatur, atque aeternum Dei decretum revocetur. Sive ergo reprobatio ponatur ex mera Divinae voluntatis libertate, omnes causas extrinsecas antegrediente, sive ex praescientia infidelitatis considerationem subsequente, perinde est: Nam nemo erit ex auditoribus, quin sit in hanc vel illam partem ab aeterno praedestinatus, ex qua in contrariam partem nunquam transferetur.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: unknown elect/non-elect — Augustine: affection of charity must will all saved; rebuke all lest they perish (De corrept. et grat.)
english: But that ought not to hinder or slow ministers' labor. As Augustine says piously and wisely (De corrept. et grat. cap. 15–16): not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, they ought to be so moved by charity that they will all to be saved. So far as concerns us, who cannot tell the predestined from the non-predestined, rebuke is to be applied to all, lest they perish or destroy others.
sections.latin: Sed hoc non debet impedire aut retardare operam ministrorum, quia, ut pie et prudenter Augustinus, De corrept. et grat. cap. 15. et 16. nescientes quis pertineat ad praedestinatorum numerum, quis non pertineat, sic affici debent charitatis affectu, ut omnes velint salvos fieri. Proinde quantum ad nos pertinet, qui praedestinatos a non praedestinatis discernere non valemus, omnibus ne pereant, vel ne alios perdant, adhibenda est correptio.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: grant diligence profits only those God absolutely wills to save — still no sluggishness: honor of co-working for the elect (1 Cor. iii. 9; 2 Tim. ii. 10); woe if not preach (1 Cor. ix. 16)
english: But come nearer still. Grant that ministers' diligence can profit only those God absolutely wills to save, who cannot perish — still neither sluggishness nor sloth is allowed. First: to profit by one's ministry those God has loved exceedingly, and whom before the world's foundations he decreed absolutely to save, is greatly honorable and desirable. Who, with any drop of piety, if he knew for certain some infant was predestined by God, would not labor the more earnestly to be counted God's fellow-worker in promoting that one's salvation (1 Cor. iii. 9)? So Paul was animated, who says all things are to be endured for the elect's sake (2 Tim. ii. 10). Further: even this can shake torpor from ministers — though God will not suffer any of the elect to perish, yet by neglecting their office they themselves incur damnable guilt, per the Apostle: Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel (1 Cor. ix. 16).
sections.latin: Verum adhuc aliquanto propius ad rem accedamus: Fac diligentiam ministrorum non posse prodesse nisi iis, quos Deus absolute vult servare, et qui perire non possunt, tamen nihil licet segnitiei neque socordiae. Primo, quia hoc ipsum prodesse suo ministerio iis, quos Deus eximie amavit, quosque ante jacta mundi fundamenta absolute servare decrevit, est valde honorificum et desiderabile. Quis enim, cui ulla inest pietatis guttula, si certo sciret aliquem infantem esse a Deo praedestinatum, non eo enixius laboraret ut in salute ejusdem promovenda Dei συνεργοὶ habeatur? 1 Cor. iii. 9. Sic Paulus animatus fuit, qui omnia propter electos sustinenda dicit, 2 Tim. ii. 10. Porro, vel illud potest ministris torporem excutere, quod licet Deus haud patietur ullum ex electis perire, tamen ipsi negligendo officium suum damnabilem reatum incurrant, juxta illud Apostoli, Vae mihi si non evangelizavero, 1 Cor. ix. 16.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: sloth cannot un-predestinate the elect, yet can harm them many ways — effects/benefits of predestination are to be advanced by ministers' diligence (Thomas)
english: Finally: no one is so impious, or so unskilled in theology, as to think ministers' sloth can make any of the predestined non-predestined, or make them fall from the glory prepared for them. Yet no one is so foolish as not to see that ministers' sloth can harm any predestined person in many ways. For though the eternal decree of God predestinating is neither procured, helped, nor hindered by any human acts, the effects of predestination — or the benefits prepared for men in it — can and ought to be advanced by ministers' diligence. So Thomas (Part. 1 q.23 a.8): Predestination does not take away second causes, but so provides for the effect that even the order of second causes lies under providence. Ministers therefore ought to know their diligence is subordinated by God to promoting the elect's salvation.
sections.latin: Denique, quamvis nemo tam impius, aut rei Theologicae imperitus sit, qui cogitet ministrorum socordia quemlibet ex praedestinatis fieri posse non praedestinatum, aut excidere posse gloria praedestinatis praeparata, tamen nemo tam imprudens est, qui non intelligat ministrorum socordiam posse variis modis cuivis praedestinato obesse. Nam licet ipsum aeternum decretum Dei praedestinantis neque procuretur, neque juvetur, neque impediatur ullis actibus humanis, tamen effecta praedestinationis, vel beneficia in praedestinatione hominibus praeparata, possunt et debent ministrorum diligentia promoveri. Unde Thomas, Part. 1. quaest. 23. artic. 8. Praedestinatio non tollit causas secundas, sed sic providet effectui ut etiam ordo causarum secundarum subjaceat providentiae. Ministri igitur scire debent suam diligentiam esse a Deo subordinatam saluti electorum promovendae.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: 'absolutely' does not mean without means — God provides for means and end; effects arise freely and contingently (Aquinas; Paul 1 Cor. ix. 27)
english: That word absolute or precise, which they hammer so often, does the adversaries no good. When God is said absolutely to have predestined, and absolutely to will the predestined's salvation, the point is not that he saves them with no means used and no conditions on men's part fulfilled. It is that of supreme mercy he looks ahead to means and end alike. He has so looked to both that the order of predestination stays certain — and once such a person is predestined, perishing and damnation are impossible — while still the effects of predestination come forth by the subject's condition and by the nature of the near causes providence set for those effects (Aquinas, ibid. art. 6): freely, contingently. So Paul, who with an eye to divine election and ordination knew he could not fall from salvation (Rom. viii. 38), did not grow idle in pressing his own: he bruises his body and brings it under, lest after preaching to others he himself somehow prove a reprobate (1 Cor. ix. 27). Divine election's firmness, then, leaves human diligence no spare office — for oneself or for others.
sections.latin: Neque quicquam juvat adversarios vocabulum illud, absolute sive praecise, quod toties inculcant. Deus enim dicitur absolute praedestinasse, et absolute velle servare praedestinatos, non quod sine ullis mediis adhibendis, aut ullis conditionibus ex parte hominum implendis, eosdem velit servare, sed quod pro summa sui misericordia tam de mediis quam de fine prospicit. De utrisque autem ita prospexit, ut quamvis ordo praedestinationis certus sit, et, posito quod talis persona praedestinetur, sit impossibile quod pereat et damnetur, tamen effectus praedestinationis producantur secundum conditionem subjecti, et secundum naturam causarum proximarum quas ad tales effectus Divina providentia ordinavit (ut inquit Aquinas, ibid. art. 6.), hoc est, libere et contingenter. Hinc Paulus, Rom. viii. 38, qui respectu electionis et ordinationis Divinae intellexit se non potuisse a salute excidere, tamen nihilo segnior evasit in salute sua promovenda, sed contundit corpus suum, et in servitutem redigit, ne quo modo cum aliis praedicavit ipse reprobus fieret, 1 Cor. ix. 27. Firmitas igitur electionis Divinae non facit ut supervacaneum sit officium diligentiae humanae, sive respectu sui ipsius sive aliorum.

sections.title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol close: negligence harms elect too; no one absolutely damned whether they repent or not; unknown whom God hardens — soft teaching (2 Tim. ii. 25); jailer analogy; absolute decrees do not cut means from end
english: Thus far of the elect. Now their objection about the reprobate — that on our view ministers' negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, who cannot be saved — is first false. It can also harm, and often does harm, the elect, while it lets them sleep for a time in their sins, and by that security provoke God's wrath and various scourges against themselves. Next: there is no reprobate whom God absolutely wills to destroy — that is (as the adversaries seem to take it) whether they repent or not, believe or not, die in their sins or not. There are many of whom God does not so have mercy as to have prepared for them special efficacious grace that will also work belief, repentance, and an end to hardening their hearts. But because ministers do not know of whom God wills to have mercy, and whom he wills to harden, they ought with all gentleness to instruct those of a contrary mind, if at any time God give them repentance (2 Tim. ii. 25). Moreover, even if it were true that ministers' negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, that does not exempt negligent ministers from guilt or capital punishment — as a jailer would not be exempt from guilt if he ran a thief through with a sword, or extinguished the means, whom the judge in his mind had absolutely decreed to damn and put to death. Finally: what they pretend — that once God has precisely decreed things thus or otherwise, care and solicitude for those same things is afterward taken up by men in vain — is most plainly that idle argument, or lazy reasoning; if we assent to it, there is nothing at all we do unwillingly (Cicero, De fato). For absolute or precise decrees of God do not cut means from the destined end, but bring both means and end under the order of a certain infallible providence. That infallibility of the thing decreed does not take away natural possibility of a contrary event — only the contrary event itself. Nor does it imply that the effect is produced without second causes, or that second causes' proper operation is broken. So the eternal secret decree of predestination and reprobation gives no one a cause of sloth — though the impious and the slothful may falsely pretext it for their idleness.
sections.latin: Hactenus de electis. Jam quod de reprobatis objiciunt, negligentiam ministrorum non posse, ex sententia nostra, nocere nisi iis quos Deus absolute vult perdere, quique non possunt servari, id primo falsum est: Nam potest etiam nocere, et saepe nocet, electis, dum patitur eos suis peccatis ad tempus indormire, et hac sua securitate iram Dei ac varia flagella contra se provocare. Dein, nemo est reprobatorum quem Deus absolute vult perdere, hoc est (ut adversarii videntur intelligere) sive poeniteant sive non poeniteant, sive credant sive non credant, sive peccatis immoriantur sive non. Sunt multi quorum Deus non sic miseretur ut praeparaverit illis gratiam specialem et efficacem atque operaturam ut credant, ut poeniteant, ut indurare sua corda desinant. Sed quia ministris ignotum est, quorum Deus vult misereri, et quos vult indurare, debent cum omni lenitate erudire eos qui contrario animo sunt affecti, si quando det illis Deus poenitentiam, etc. 2 Tim. ii. 25. Adhaec, si verum esset, negligentiam ministrorum non posse nocere nisi iis, quos Deus absolute vult perdere, tamen hoc non eximit negligentes ministros vel a culpa vel a poena capitali; sicuti custos carceris a culpa non eximeretur, si latronem gladio transfoderet, aut media extingueret, quem judex apud animum suum absolute decrevisset damnare, et morte afficere. Denique, quod obtendunt, rebus praecise sic vel aliter a Deo semel decretis, curam et solicitudinem earundem rerum frustra postmodum ab hominibus suscipi, est planissime ignava illa ratio, sive ἀργολογία, cui si assentiamur, nihil est omnino quod agamus invita, ut inquit Cicero De fato. Absoluta enim sive praecisa Dei decreta non praescindunt media a fine destinato, sed et media et finem ad infallibilis cujusdam providentiae ordinem reducunt. Neque haec infallibilitas rei decretae tollit naturalem possibilitatem ad eventum contrarium, sed ipsum eventum contrarium: neque etiam innuit aut effectum sine causis secundis producendum, aut propriam operationem secundarum causarum infringendam. Aeternum et arcanum igitur praedestinationis et reprobationis decretum nemini praebet causam socordiae, quamvis impii et socordes possint hoc suae ignaviae falso praetexere.
